The question calls them ‘seven ethical requirements’, but recital 27 of the EU AI Act identifies the 2019 AI HLEG guidance as seven **non-binding ethical principles**: human agency and oversight; technical robustness and safety; privacy and data governance; transparency; diversity, non-discrimination and fairness; societal and environmental well-being; and accountability. The recital expressly distinguishes those guidelines from the Regulation’s legally binding requirements [EU AI Act PDF, p. 8, recital 27].

By contrast, the Act imposes legal duties for high-risk AI systems. Examples in the supplied text include establishing and maintaining a risk-management system (Article 9, p. 56), applying data-governance practices to relevant training, validation and testing data (Article 10, p. 57), designing systems for effective human oversight (Article 14, p. 60), and provider duties such as ensuring compliance with Section 2 (Article 16, p. 62). These are examples, not an exhaustive list [EU AI Act PDF, pp. 56–57, 60, 62].

In short: the seven principles are broad, non-binding ethical guidance; the Act’s high-risk requirements are specific legal obligations. They can address overlapping values, but they are not interchangeable checklists.
